title: Information Content of the Cosmic Web
summary: We present an information-theoretic analysis of the Cosmic Web that goes beyond the scalar density contrast and exploits the full structure of the tidal deformation tensor. The three eigenvalues (lambda1, lambda2, lambda3) of the tidal Hessian furnish a natural morphological classifier: clusters, filaments, walls, and voids correspond to (+,+,+), (+,+,-), (+,-,-), and (-,-,-) sign patterns, and their joint probability distribution function (PDF), known analytically in the linear regime from Doroshkevich (1970), defines a continuous Shannon entropy that quantifies the information encoded in the geometry of large-scale structure. Additional information resides in the shear invariants Q = Trace(T2) and A = Trace(T3), which are algebraically independent of the density contrast delta and capture anisotropic deformation invisible to the density alone. The information dimension of each morphological component is related to its Hausdorff (fractal) dimension through the multifractal formalism: clusters (DH = 1.2), filaments (DH = 1.8), walls (DH = 2.5), and voids (DH = 3) define a spectrum of generalized Renyi dimensions Dq, whose q = 1 limit recovers the Shannon information dimension. The resulting entropy budget identifies filaments as the dominant information carriers of the mater distribution, while the tidal eigenvalue entropy is maximized in wall-like configurations near the saddle points of the gravitational potential. We also compute the redshift evolution of the multifractal entropy and derive its relation to the linear growth rate f(z), providing an independent constraint complementary to redshift-space-distortion measurements of f*sigma8.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an information-theoretic analysis of the Cosmic Web using the tidal deformation tensor eigenvalues and shear invariants, deriving Shannon entropy, multifractal dimensions, and redshift evolution of entropy to characterize cosmic structure morphology beyond the standard density contrast.
AI.motivation: To move beyond scalar density contrast analysis and exploit the full tidal deformation tensor to capture anisotropic morphological information in the Cosmic Web, quantifying how much information is encoded in geometric structures (clusters, filaments, walls, voids).
AI.method: Uses the three eigenvalues (λ1, λ2, λ3) of the tidal Hessian as morphological classifiers with sign patterns; employs the Doroshkevich (1970) joint PDF for Shannon entropy; incorporates shear invariants Q=Tr(T²) and A=Tr(T³) for anisotropic deformation; applies multifractal formalism linking Hausdorff dimensions to generalized Rényi dimensions Dq.
AI.result: Filaments are the dominant information carriers; tidal eigenvalue entropy is maximized in wall-like configurations near saddle points of the gravitational potential; clusters (DH=1.2), filaments (DH=1.8), walls (DH=2.5), voids (DH=3) define the fractal dimension spectrum; entropy redshift evolution relates to linear growth rate f(z).
AI.conclusion: The tidal eigenvalue entropy and multifractal formalism provide a complementary constraint to redshift-space-distortion measurements of fσ₈, offering a novel probe of cosmic structure growth and morphology.

title: Still non-accelerating: age-bias correction in supernova cosmology is robust to host-progenitor age mapping
summary: We re-examine the claim by Wiseman et al. (2026) that progenitor-age bias has a negligible impact on cosmological inferences from Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia). We show that their inferred host-age-Hubble residual (HR) slope is severely underestimated because their combined SN Ia sample spans an unusually wide redshift range ($0.04 < z < 0.42$), over which the mean host age evolves by $\sim$\,3 Gyr. As a result, SNe Ia spanning substantial host-age differences are effectively assigned similar HR values prior to regression, artificially flattening the inferred age-HR relation. In addition, their application of the Pantheon+ host-mass correction further suppresses the slope, but the underlying dust model is highly incompatible with the measured dust attenuation curves of galaxies. We also demonstrate that our age bias correction is robust to uncertainties in host-progenitor age mapping arising from different choices of the SN Ia delay-time distribution. The reduced progenitor-age evolution argued by Wiseman et al. (2026) must, by the same logic, be accompanied by a steeper inferred progenitor-age-HR slope. When these two effects are consistently combined in computing the redshift-dependent magnitude correction, the final correction, and hence the resulting cosmological impact, remain largely unchanged from Son et al. (2025).

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines Wiseman et al. (2026) and finds that their claim of negligible progenitor-age bias on Type Ia supernova cosmology is flawed due to (1) redshift evolution of host ages across a wide range artificially flattening the age-HR slope, (2) an incompatible dust model in their host-mass correction, and (3) that when corrected, the age bias impact remains consistent with Son et al. (2025).
AI.motivation: To critically re-evaluate the claim by Wiseman et al. (2026) that progenitor-age bias has negligible cosmological impact on SNe Ia, and to demonstrate methodological flaws leading to underestimated age-HR slope and correction.
AI.method: Re-analysis of the Wiseman et al. (2026) SN Ia sample spanning $0.04 < z < 0.42$, examining host-age-redshift evolution, testing the Pantheon+ host-mass correction dust model against measured dust attenuation curves, and assessing robustness of age bias correction against different delay-time distribution assumptions.
AI.result: Wiseman et al. (2026) severely underestimated the host-age-Hubble residual slope due to host-age evolution across redshift and incompatible dust modeling; the progenitor-age-HR slope must be steeper when age evolution is consistently accounted for, but the combined redshift-dependent magnitude correction remains similar to Son et al. (2025).
AI.conclusion: The claim of reduced progenitor-age evolution by Wiseman et al. (2026) is invalid due to methodological issues; the cosmological impact of progenitor-age bias remains significant and consistent with prior work (Son et al. 2025).

title: Machine Learning applications to Galaxy Clusters
comment: Invited chapter for the book "Machine Learning Techniques for Astrophysics and Cosmology" (Eds. C. Bambi, V. Kashyap, S. Shashank and N. Yoshida, Springer Singapore, expected to be published in 2027
summary: This chapter reviews the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques to the study of galaxy clusters, covering both theoretical developments and their use as tools to infer cluster properties from a variety of observational tracers. We discuss recent advances in mass estimation from SZ, X-ray, optical, and dynamical data, highlighting the ability of AI methods to capture non-linear features, projection effects, and complex cluster morphologies beyond more classical approaches. In addition, we present other emerging applications, including the emulation of baryonic physics from N-body simulations, the characterization of dynamical states and mergers, and the analysis of the diffuse components such as the intracluster light. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of simulations in training these models, the impact of baryonic modelling, and the need for a robust uncertainty quantification and interpretability. Finally, we outline current limitations and future prospects, stressing the importance of combining flexible simulation strategies with AI techniques to fully exploit next-generation surveys for precision cosmology.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews AI applications in galaxy cluster studies, covering mass estimation across multiple observational tracers (SZ, X-ray, optical, dynamical), emulation of baryonic physics, dynamical state characterization, and analysis of diffuse components. It emphasizes simulation-based model training, baryonic modeling impact, uncertainty quantification, and interpretability, while outlining future prospects for next-generation cosmological surveys.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive review of how AI techniques are advancing the study of galaxy clusters, addressing limitations of classical approaches in capturing non-linear features, projection effects, and complex morphologies, thereby enabling more precise cosmological inference from next-generation surveys.
AI.method: Review of AI methods applied to multi-wavelength cluster data (SZ, X-ray, optical, dynamical) for mass estimation; emulation of baryonic physics from N-body simulations; characterization of dynamical states and mergers; analysis of diffuse intracluster light. Emphasis on simulation-based training and uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: AI methods demonstrate superior ability to capture non-linear features, projection effects, and complex cluster morphologies compared to classical approaches. Emerging applications include baryonic physics emulation, merger/dynamical state characterization, and intracluster light analysis.
AI.conclusion: Combining flexible simulation strategies with AI techniques is essential for fully exploiting next-generation surveys in precision cosmology, though robust uncertainty quantification and interpretability remain key challenges.

title: Blue-tilted Runnings and the JWST Early Galaxy Tension
summary: The recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations reported the unexpectedly large abundance of massive galaxies with stellar masses of $\sim 10^{10}~M_{\odot}$ at high redshifts $z \simeq 6.5 - 9$ compared with the prediction of the standard $Λ$CDM model. As a possible solution to the tension, we consider a blue-tilted spectrum of density perturbations with a positive running. We find that, for $α_s \simeq 0.2$ and $β_s \simeq 0.2$, a joint analysis with CMB observations shows that the tension can be resolved at the 1$σ$ confidence level. Such a blue-tilted spectrum is also plausible from the perspective of primordial black hole formation on much smaller scales in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: JWST observed more massive galaxies at high redshifts than ΛCDM predicts. This tension can be resolved at 1σ by a blue-tilted density perturbation spectrum (α_s ≈ 0.2, β_s ≈ 0.2) consistent with CMB data and primordial black hole formation.
AI.motivation: JWST observations reveal an unexpectedly high abundance of massive galaxies (~10¹⁰ M☉) at redshifts z ≈ 6.5–9, challenging standard ΛCDM predictions and motivating a search for modifications to the primordial power spectrum.
AI.method: The authors propose a blue-tilted primordial power spectrum with positive running (α_s ≈ 0.2, β_s ≈ 0.2) and perform a joint analysis with CMB observations to test consistency with the JWST galaxy abundance data.
AI.result: The blue-tilted spectrum resolves the JWST massive galaxy tension at the 1σ confidence level while remaining compatible with CMB constraints.
AI.conclusion: A blue-tilted primordial spectrum is a viable solution to the JWST excess of massive high-z galaxies and is also plausible from the perspective of primordial black hole formation on smaller scales.

title: (LRDs)$^2$: The Low-ReDshift Little Red Dots Survey. II. DESI DR1 Sample
comment: Main text 28 pages; 17 figures. Submitted to the ApJ. Comments are welcome. Data are available on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20309303
summary: JWST has revealed a substantial population of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at $z>4$, challenging conventional AGN frameworks. However, the low-redshift regime remains largely unexplored. In the second paper of the (LRDs)$^2$ series, we present a systematic selection from DESI DR1 and identify 27 LRDs at $z=0.2-0.9$, yielding a number density lower limit of $7.5 \times 10^{-10}$ cMpc$^{-3}$. We conducted near-IR spectroscopic follow-up observations for 18 of them, revealing their full SED shapes and emission lines. These low-$z$ LRDs share the hallmark properties of their high-$z$ counterparts: compact morphology, V-shaped UV-optical continua, broad Balmer emission with extreme decrements (median H$α$/H$β\sim 16$), frequent Balmer absorption (67%), and blackbody-like optical-to-near-IR continua. All have low metallicity, occupy the same regions in the BPT diagram as high-$z$ LRDs, and have softer ionizing spectra than typical AGNs. The consistency between low-$z$ and high-$z$ LRD properties indicates the same physical processes at work. The correlation between broad-line Balmer luminosity and $L_{5100}$ deviates from that of local type-1 AGNs, limiting the direct application of local BH mass calibrations. Ionized [O III] outflows are ubiquitous (78%). One LRD at $z=0.196$, J1717+3807, shows robust long-term variability in $i$ and WISE bands. The optical-to-NIR continua of LRDs reveal a wide range of temperatures $\sim 2000-4700$ K (peak $0.6-1.5$ $μ$m), with a subset showing cooler and larger envelopes than those at high $z$. Low-$z$ LRDs serve not only as proximate laboratories for probing the nature of LRDs, but also trace the cosmic evolution of this population from the cosmic dawn to the present day.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically identifies 27 Little Red Dots (LRDs) at low redshift (z=0.2-0.9) using DESI DR1 data, conducts near-IR spectroscopic follow-up for 18, and finds they share hallmark properties with high-z LRDs—compact morphology, V-shaped UV-optical continua, broad Balmer emission with extreme decrements, Balmer absorption, low metallicity, and ubiquitous ionized outflows. One object shows long-term variability. Their SEDs reveal a wide temperature range (2000-4700 K), and their broad-line Balmer luminosity relation deviates from local type-1 AGN calibrations, establishing low-z LRDs as proximate analogs for studying the population across cosmic time.
AI.motivation: JWST has revealed abundant LRDs at z>4, challenging conventional AGN models, but the low-redshift LRD population remains largely unexplored, limiting our understanding of their nature and cosmic evolution.
AI.method: Authors systematically selected LRDs from DESI DR1, yielding 27 candidates at z=0.2-0.9, and conducted near-IR spectroscopic follow-up for 18 objects, analyzing their SED shapes, emission lines, BPT diagnostics, Balmer decrements, outflows, variability, and black hole mass calibrations.
AI.result: 27 LRDs identified at low redshift with number density lower limit 7.5×10⁻¹⁰ cMpc⁻³. They share hallmark high-z LRD properties: compact morphology, V-shaped continua, broad Balmer emission with extreme Hα/Hβ~16, 67% Balmer absorption, low metallicity, soft ionizing spectra, and 78% show [O III] outflows. One object (J1717+3807) exhibits long-term variability. SEDs span 2000-4700 K temperatures. The broad-line Balmer luminosity vs. L₅₁₀₀ relation deviates from local type-1 AGNs.
AI.conclusion: Low-z LRDs are consistent with high-z LRDs, indicating the same physical processes operate across redshifts. They serve as proximate laboratories for probing LRD nature and trace the population's cosmic evolution from the cosmic dawn to the present day. Standard local BH mass calibrations cannot be directly applied to LRDs.

title: Dark photon -- Assisted Primordial Magnetogenesis
summary: Magnetic fields observed across cosmic scales are difficult to explain within conventional physics. A primordial origin is, thus, often assumed. While a nonminimal coupling of the inflaton with the electromagnetic field could theoretically generate magnetic fields of about $10^{-13}$ G, this approach faces significant issues, including strong-coupling and backreaction problems. ``Dark photons", arising naturally in hidden-sector extensions of the Standard Model, provide a well-motivated framework for addressing various cosmic as well as particle physics issues. We demonstrate that coupling dark photons with standard ones can result in adequate magnetogenesis without the limitations of existing models. This minimal mechanism may also provide insights into unresolved cosmic mysteries.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a magnetogenesis mechanism using dark photons coupled to standard photons, avoiding strong-coupling and backreaction issues that plague conventional inflationary models, and potentially explaining observed cosmic magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: Observed cosmic magnetic fields lack sufficient explanation within conventional physics, motivating a primordial origin. Existing inflationary magnetogenesis via nonminimal inflaton-photon coupling suffers from strong-coupling and backreaction problems.
AI.method: The authors introduce dark photons from hidden-sector extensions of the Standard Model and demonstrate that coupling dark photons to standard photons generates magnetic fields without the limitations of previous models.
AI.result: The proposed dark photon mechanism produces adequate magnetogenesis (~10^{-13} G) while avoiding strong-coupling and backreaction issues inherent in nonminimal inflaton coupling approaches.
AI.conclusion: Dark photon-mediated magnetogenesis offers a minimal, viable primordial mechanism for cosmic magnetic fields, and may additionally shed light on other unresolved cosmic mysteries.

title: Investigating central star formation in local AGN host galaxies: is there tension between coeval growth and AGN feedback?
comment: 15 pages, 17 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: It has been argued that supermassive black holes (BHs) coevolve with the central parts of galaxies, as a result of the common fuel for both the BH and star formation in the galaxy central region, as supported by the particularly significant relation between BH growth and the central mass density within 1 kpc found among star-forming galaxies. In the context of this scenario, one would naturally expect a close observational link between AGN activity and star formation activity in the central regions, e.g., the surface star formation rate density in the central 1 kpc region ($Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$), as the manifestation of coeval growth. With ~3000 galaxies in the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey that have X-ray coverage from SRG/eROSITA, XMM-Newton, or Chandra, we studied how the X-ray AGN fraction varies with $Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$. We found that the fraction of X-ray AGNs with relatively higher specific BH accretion rates increases with $Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$, consistent with the expectation. Comparison of the mean star formation rate surface density ($Σ_{\rm SFR}$) profiles of the host galaxies of these AGNs and normal galaxies sharing similar properties reveals elevated $Σ_{\rm SFR}$ in AGN hosts across the entire central region. As for optically-selected AGNs, their hosts also tend to show high $Σ_{\rm SFR}$ in the central regions on average compared to normal galaxies, but are discrepant with X-ray AGNs in terms of the trend of AGN fraction vs. $Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$, which can be explained by selection effects. While these general trends all support the coeval growth scenario, they do not contradict observational evidence for AGN feedback, as the time-averaged effects from local AGN feedback are modest in star-forming regions.

AI.tldr: This study uses ~3000 MaNGA galaxies with X-ray data to show that AGN fraction increases with central star formation rate density (Σ_SFR, 1 kpc), supporting the coevolution of supermassive black holes and their host galaxies, though selection effects cause differences between X-ray and optically-selected AGNs, and the results do not contradict AGN feedback models.
AI.motivation: To test the BH-galaxy coevolution scenario by examining the observational link between AGN activity and central star formation rate density, particularly the relationship between X-ray AGN fraction and Σ_SFR within 1 kpc.
AI.method: Analyzed ~3000 galaxies from the MaNGA survey with X-ray coverage from SRG/eROSITA, XMM-Newton, or Chandra; measured X-ray AGN fraction as a function of Σ_SFR, 1 kpc; compared Σ_SFR profiles of AGN hosts vs. normal galaxies; contrasted X-ray-selected and optically-selected AGNs.
AI.result: X-ray AGN fraction with higher specific BH accretion rates increases with Σ_SFR, 1 kpc; AGN hosts show elevated Σ_SFR across entire central region compared to normal galaxies; optically-selected AGN hosts also show high central Σ_SFR, but their AGN fraction vs. Σ_SFR trend differs from X-ray AGNs due to selection effects.
AI.conclusion: The results support the coeval growth scenario between BHs and galaxies, while not contradicting evidence for AGN feedback, as local AGN feedback effects are modest in star-forming regions when time-averaged.

title: Signatures of Modified Gravity Below $\mathcal{O}(10)$ Mpc in a Dynamical Dark Energy Background
summary: Cosmological data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryon acoustic oscillations, and Type Ia supernovae suggest that the component driving the accelerated expansion of the Universe may be dynamical at the $\sim 2.5$-$3σ$ CL. The best-fit CPL model produces a level of cosmic structure similar to that of $Λ$CDM, with both models exhibiting mild tension with redshift-space distortion data. In this {\it Letter}, we parametrize possible departures of the effective gravitational coupling from Newton's constant in the late Universe, below a comoving scale $λ_c$, using two redshift bins, $0 \leq z < 1$ and $1 \leq z \leq 3$. We then determine the optimal values of $λ_c$ and the amplitude of these deviations from General Relativity, assuming a background with dynamical dark energy in CPL form. We find that, in order to achieve the required suppression of structure growth at low redshifts while remaining consistent with CMB constraints -- primarily from the late-time ISW effect at low $\ell$ and lensing at high $\ell$ -- modified gravity effects must appear on scales smaller than $λ_c \sim \mathcal{O}(10)\,\mathrm{Mpc}$. Using Planck PR4, DESI DR2, Pantheon+ (or DES-Dovekie) and redshift-space distortions data we confirm that a CPL background with standard gravity is moderately preferred over $Λ$CDM; this preference strengthens to a mildly strong level when modified gravity effects are included. This enhancement leaves the CPL parameters largely unchanged, but shifts them slightly further into the quintom region.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether dynamical dark energy (CPL model) or modified gravity can better explain cosmic acceleration, using CMB, BAO, SNe, and RSD data. It finds that modified gravity effects must operate on scales <~10 Mpc to suppress structure growth consistently with CMB constraints. A CPL background with standard gravity is moderately preferred over ΛCDM, and mildly strongly preferred when modified gravity is included, pushing parameters slightly into the quintom region.
AI.motivation: Cosmological data suggest that dark energy may be dynamical (~2.5-3σ CL), motivating a test of whether modified gravity or dynamical dark energy better resolves tensions in structure growth data, particularly with redshift-space distortions.
AI.method: Parametrizes deviations of the effective gravitational coupling from Newton's constant below a comoving scale λ_c using two redshift bins (0≤z<1 and 1≤z≤3). Assumes a CPL dynamical dark energy background and fits λ_c and deviation amplitudes using Planck PR4, DESI DR2, Pantheon+/DES-Dovekie, and RSD data.
AI.result: Modified gravity effects must occur on scales <~10 Mpc to suppress low-redshift structure growth while matching CMB constraints (ISW and lensing). A CPL background with standard gravity is moderately preferred over ΛCDM; including modified gravity strengthens this preference to mildly strong, with CPL parameters shifting slightly into the quintom region.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical dark energy (CPL) is moderately preferred over ΛCDM, and this preference becomes mildly strong when allowing for late-time modified gravity on small scales (<~10 Mpc). The combined scenario pushes dark energy into the quintom regime while leaving CPL parameters largely unchanged.

title: Constraining Spatial Curvature with Priors from Swampland Conjectures
summary: We study a string-motivated theoretical prior on the quintessential dark energy model with exponential potential, \( V(φ) = V_0 e^{-λφ} \), allowing for non-zero spatial curvature. First, we formulate the corresponding dynamical system and investigate its cosmological evolution numerically, illustrating the phase-space behaviour and the influence of curvature on the background dynamics. In open universes (\( Ω_k > 0 \)), it has been suggested that a curvature-related fixed point may support accelerated expansion even for relatively steep potentials compatible with swampland considerations. Next, we explicitly impose swampland-motivated priors on the slope parameter $λ$, restricting it to values consistent with the de Sitter conjecture that excludes the (curved) $Λ$CDM limit. Furthermore, we restrict our considerations to the range of field excursion that is consistent with the swampland distance conjecture. Our primary interest is the possibility that such theoretically-motivated priors may shift values of cosmological parameters inferred by observational data, compared with the standard analysis based on theory-agnostic priors such as a sufficiently wide flat prior. We examine this possibility using a combination of Planck CMB data, DESI BAO measurements, and recent Type Ia supernova samples, performing a Bayesian inference of the model parameters. Our analysis indicates that the swampland-motivated prior mildly shifts the values of $Ω_k$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quintessential dark energy with an exponential potential in non-flat universes, imposing swampland-motivated priors (de Sitter conjecture and distance conjecture) on the model parameters. Using Planck CMB, DESI BAO, and Type Ia supernova data, Bayesian inference shows that these theoretical priors mildly shift the inferred values of spatial curvature $Ω_k$ compared to standard theory-agnostic priors.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether theoretically-motivated priors from string theory (swampland conjectures) can shift cosmological parameter inferences (particularly spatial curvature) compared to standard flat priors, in the context of quintessence dark energy with exponential potential.
AI.method: (1) Formulate the dynamical system for quintessence with exponential potential in curved universes. (2) Perform numerical evolution and phase-space analysis, identifying curvature-related fixed points. (3) Impose swampland-motivated priors: de Sitter conjecture restricts the slope $λ$ (excluding curved $Λ$CDM limit), and distance conjecture limits field excursion. (4) Bayesian inference using Planck CMB, DESI BAO, and Type Ia supernova data.
AI.result: The swampland-motivated priors mildly shift the inferred values of the spatial curvature parameter $Ω_k$ compared to the standard analysis using theory-agnostic (e.g., wide flat) priors.
AI.conclusion: String theory-inspired priors can have a non-negligible impact on cosmological parameter inference, particularly for spatial curvature, suggesting that theory-motivated priors should be considered in cosmological data analysis beyond standard flat-prior approaches.

title: Decomposing cool stellar populations with H-band spectral fluctuations: Long-period variable stars in NGC 5128 and carbon stars in NGC 5102
summary: We analyse new H-band integral-field unit observations of two galaxies at ~4 Mpc, using a principal components analysis of pixel spectra to probe their giant star content. In both galaxies, the signals arise in near-resolved point-like sources without large-scale variation, consistent with each pixel sampling stars randomly from a common underlying population. In the (mostly) old bulge of NGC 5128, the observed pixel-to-pixel variation is dominated by a component with a mid-M giant spectrum with prominent CO bandheads. We also recover a smoother second spectral component, apparently driven by contributions from later spectral types. This component is not present in predictions from Poisson-sampled models of old stellar populations; we suggest that it arises from the cool phases of long-period variable stars. (An appendix provides direct evidence for such variables in complementary two-epoch MUSE observations.) In the contrasting galaxy NGC 5102, where a post-starburst stellar population is known to be present, we again find two distinct components. As before, the first component carries the CO bands typical of M-giants. The second eigenspectrum in this younger galaxy shows a strong 1.77 micron C2 bandhead, a feature which is characteristic of carbon stars. Our results highlight the ability of integral field data to access information beyond the total spectrum, even when individual stars cannot be classically resolved.

AI.tldr: Using H-band IFU observations of two ~4 Mpc galaxies (NGC 5128 and NGC 5102), PCA of pixel spectra reveals that pixel-to-pixel variations are dominated by point-like sources. In NGC 5128's old bulge, the first component is mid-M giant spectra (CO bandheads) and a second smoother component attributed to long-period variable stars. In NGC 5102 (post-starburst), the first component is again M-giants, but the second shows a strong 1.77 μm C₂ bandhead from carbon stars, demonstrating that IFU data can extract information beyond the integrated spectrum even when stars are not resolved.
AI.motivation: To probe the giant star content in nearby galaxies using IFU observations beyond what integrated spectra can provide, even when individual stars cannot be classically resolved.
AI.method: H-band integral-field unit observations of two galaxies at ~4 Mpc (NGC 5128 and NGC 5102) analyzed via principal components analysis (PCA) of pixel spectra. Complementary two-epoch MUSE observations were used as an appendix for direct evidence of long-period variables.
AI.result: In NGC 5128 (old bulge), two components are found: (1) mid-M giant spectrum with CO bandheads, (2) a smoother component from later spectral types, attributed to cool phases of long-period variable stars. In NGC 5102 (post-starburst), similar two components, but the second shows a strong 1.77 μm C₂ bandhead characteristic of carbon stars, reflecting the younger stellar population.
AI.conclusion: IFU data can access information beyond the total integrated spectrum, enabling the study of stellar content variations even when individual stars remain classically unresolved.

title: Machine Learning Techniques for Astrophysics and Cosmology: Lyman-$α$ forest
comment: Invited chapter for the edited book "Machine Learning Techniques for Astrophysics and Cosmology" (Eds. Cosimo Bambi, Vinay Kashyap, Swarnim Shashank, Naoki Yoshida, Springer Singapore, expected in 2026). Submitted version
summary: The Lyman-$α$ forest refers to the series of absorption features observed in the spectra of distant quasars that are produced by neutral hydrogen in the intergalactic medium. Observed over a wide range of redshifts with both ground- and space-based facilities, the Lyman-$α$ forest provides a powerful probe of numerous physical processes, including the thermal state of intergalactic gas, the timing and topology of cosmic reionization, the expansion history of the Universe, the growth of cosmic structure, massive neutrinos, and the nature of dark matter. This chapter reviews the transformative impact of machine-learning techniques on Lyman-$α$ forest analyses, particularly in overcoming the computational and methodological limitations of traditional approaches. We discuss a broad range of machine-learning applications, including the automated characterization of individual absorption systems, improved reconstruction of the intrinsic quasar continuum, accelerated emulation of hydrodynamical simulations, and the development of simulation-based analyses, field-level inference methods, and three-dimensional reconstruction techniques for the underlying matter density field. As current and upcoming surveys continue to increase both the volume and precision of Lyman-$α$ forest observations, ML-driven pipelines are becoming an essential component of next-generation astrophysical and cosmological analyses.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews how machine learning is transforming Lyman-α forest analysis—overcoming computational and methodological limits of traditional approaches—by enabling automated absorption-system characterization, quasar continuum reconstruction, simulation emulation, simulation-based inference, field-level inference, and 3D matter density reconstruction, which is essential for next-generation surveys.
AI.motivation: The Lyman-α forest is a powerful cosmological probe (sensitive to reionization, expansion history, structure growth, neutrinos, dark matter), but traditional analysis methods face computational and methodological limitations. The growing volume and precision of observations from current and upcoming surveys demand more efficient and accurate approaches.
AI.method: The paper surveys a broad range of ML applications: (1) automated characterization of individual absorption systems, (2) improved reconstruction of the intrinsic quasar continuum, (3) accelerated emulation of hydrodynamical simulations, (4) simulation-based inference, (5) field-level inference, and (6) 3D reconstruction of the underlying matter density field.
AI.result: ML-driven pipelines overcome the computational bottlenecks of traditional Lyman-α forest analyses, enabling automated, scalable, and more precise extraction of astrophysical and cosmological information from increasingly large observational datasets.
AI.conclusion: ML-driven pipelines are becoming an essential component of next-generation astrophysical and cosmological analyses as surveys continue to increase both the volume and precision of Lyman-α forest observations.

title: A Magnetized Black Hole Envelope Model for Little Red Dots
summary: Recent observations have revealed a unique class of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), termed little red dots (LRDs). These objects are hypothesized to be powered by massive black holes rapidly accreting in dense gaseous environments. Theoretical studies suggest that the circum-nuclear gas can form an optically thick black hole envelope (BHE), whose structure resembles the atmospheres of convective stars near the Hayashi limit. Given that such cool stars typically generate magnetic fields, we propose a dynamical and spectral model for an LRD enshrouded by a magnetized BHE. Assuming spherical free-fall accretion onto a rotating, magnetized BHE, our model accounts for key observational properties of LRDs. We propose that the Doppler component of broad emission lines originates from plasma clumps co-rotating within the BHE magnetosphere. Including additional broadening due to electron scattering allows the resulting line profile to be fitted by a combination of a Gaussian core and an exponential tail. This model can reproduce Doppler components up to a few thousand ${\rm km~s^{-1}}$. We suggest that conventional black hole mass estimation methods based on the virial relation may yield erroneous results. Furthermore, our model is consistent with X-ray non-detections in LRDs. We evaluate the X-ray luminosities of two potential sources: the post-shock region of accretion shocks and a magnetically heated corona. We find that these X-ray luminosities are constrained to $\lesssim 10^{41}~{\rm erg~s^{-1}}$ across a wide range of black hole masses ($10^5 M_\odot \lesssim M_{\rm BH}\lesssim 10^7M_\odot$) and accretion rates, consistent with current upper limits on X-ray emission.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that little red dots (LRDs) — a unique class of AGNs — are powered by massive black holes accreting within a magnetized, optically thick black hole envelope (BHE). The model explains broad emission line profiles via co-rotating plasma clumps and electron scattering, and predicts X-ray luminosities below current detection limits, suggesting conventional black hole mass estimates may be unreliable.
AI.motivation: To explain the observational properties of little red dots (LRDs) — a newly discovered class of AGNs — by developing a theoretical model that incorporates a magnetized, optically thick black hole envelope, and to address inconsistencies in black hole mass estimation and X-ray non-detection.
AI.method: The model assumes spherical free-fall accretion onto a rotating, magnetized black hole envelope (BHE) whose structure is analogous to convective stellar atmospheres near the Hayashi limit. Broad emission lines are modeled as Doppler components from co-rotating plasma clumps within the BHE magnetosphere, with additional broadening from electron scattering. X-ray luminosities are estimated from accretion shock post-shock regions and magnetically heated coronae.
AI.result: The model reproduces Doppler components up to a few thousand km/s. It finds that X-ray luminosities from both accretion shocks and magnetically heated coronae are ≤10^41 erg/s for black hole masses 10^5–10^7 M⊙ across a wide range of accretion rates, consistent with observed X-ray non-detections in LRDs.
AI.conclusion: LRDs can be understood as accreting black holes enshrouded by magnetized, optically thick envelopes. Standard virial-based black hole mass estimates are likely erroneous for these objects. The model naturally explains the absence of strong X-ray emission in LRDs.

title: The impact of evolving dark energy on the Weyl potential measured from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 data
summary: Measurements from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) Year 3 data have shown that the Weyl potential -- the sum of the spatial and temporal distortions of the geometry -- evolves more slowly than predicted by General Relativity, assuming a $Λ$CDM background evolution. An evolving dark energy with a phantom crossing, as preferred by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), is expected to decrease the depth of the gravitational potentials through a stronger acceleration than in $Λ$CDM, potentially solving the tension with General Relativity. In this paper, we show that $w_0w_a$CDM models indeed reduce the tension with respect to $Λ$CDM, down to a level of $1.6-2.2σ$, depending on the treatment of CMB lensing. This reduction is not due to an increase in the Weyl potential's uncertainties, but truly to the impact of the evolving background on the theoretical predictions in General Relativity. More data are needed to robustly determine if evolving dark energy fully explains the low value of the Weyl potential at intermediate redshifts, or if modifications of gravity or interactions in the dark sector are needed, which could simultaneously stabilize the phantom crossing indicated by DESI.

AI.tldr: Evolving dark energy (w0waCDM) reduces tension between DES Year 3 Weyl potential measurements and General Relativity from ~3σ to 1.6-2.2σ, without relying on increased uncertainties, but further data needed to distinguish between dark energy, modified gravity, or dark sector interactions.
AI.motivation: DES Year 3 data showed the Weyl potential evolves more slowly than predicted by GR with ΛCDM background, creating a tension. DESI's preference for phantom-crossing dark energy suggests this evolving background might resolve the tension, motivating investigation into whether w0waCDM models can explain the discrepancy.
AI.method: The authors compare theoretical predictions of the Weyl potential evolution in w0waCDM models (with phantom crossing dark energy) against DES Year 3 measurements, analyzing the tension reduction relative to ΛCDM under different treatments of CMB lensing.
AI.result: w0waCDM models reduce the tension with GR from the ΛCDM level down to 1.6-2.2σ, depending on CMB lensing treatment. The reduction is due to the evolving background's impact on theoretical predictions, not increased uncertainties in the Weyl potential.
AI.conclusion: Evolving dark energy partially resolves the Weyl potential tension, but more data are needed to determine whether dark energy, modified gravity, or dark sector interactions are responsible, especially given DESI's phantom crossing preference.

title: Towards precision cosmology with Void x CMB correlations (II): Impact of mock catalogs on the Void x CMB lensing signal
summary: Gravitational lensing by large-scale structure imprints secondary anisotropies on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) that can be exploited to probe cosmology. In particular, cosmic voids produce a characteristic lensing signature detectable through Void x CMB cross-correlations. This signal has been robustly measured in the past but its cosmological constraining power remains limited by the incomplete knowledge of how methodological choices affect its measurement and by its uncertain dependence on cosmological parameters. Using a set of validated Roman mock catalogs, we first quantify how mock construction impacts the measured signal and then forecast the capabilities of Roman, in combination with current and upcoming CMB surveys such as Planck, SO and CMB-S4-like experiments. We analyze the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) for different void definitions (2D and 3D), stacking approaches (rescaled versus non-rescaled profiles), CMB map filtering schemes and noise levels. In contrast to galaxy and void statistics, we find that the Void x CMB lensing signal is less sensitive to the choice of mock catalog, indicating that future tensions with data are unlikely to stem from mock inaccuracies alone. The highest S/N is achieved for 2D voids with rescaled profiles. We forecast S/N ~13$σ$ (8$σ$) for 2D (3D) Roman voids combined with Planck, increasing to 22$σ$ (13$σ$) for SO and 31$σ$ (18$σ$) for CMB-S4-like surveys. While the cosmological dependence of this observable remains to be quantified, Roman together with next-generation of LSS and CMB surveys opens a path toward the first direct cosmological constraints from Void x CMB lensing.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how gravitational lensing of the CMB by cosmic voids can be used for cosmology. Using Roman mock catalogs, the authors quantify how methodological choices (void definition, stacking, filtering) affect the Void x CMB lensing signal and forecast signal-to-noise ratios for Roman combined with Planck, SO, and CMB-S4-like surveys. They find that 2D voids with rescaled profiles achieve the highest S/N (~13σ with Planck, up to ~31σ with CMB-S4). The signal is robust to mock catalog choices.
AI.motivation: Gravitational lensing by large-scale structure imprints secondary anisotropies on the CMB that can probe cosmology. Cosmic voids produce a characteristic lensing signal measurable via Void x CMB cross-correlations, but its cosmological constraining power is limited by incomplete knowledge of how methodological choices affect measurement and by its uncertain cosmological parameter dependence.
AI.method: Using validated Roman mock catalogs, the authors quantify how mock construction impacts the measured Void x CMB lensing signal and forecast Roman's capabilities combined with Planck, SO, and CMB-S4-like surveys. They analyze S/N for different void definitions (2D vs 3D), stacking approaches (rescaled vs non-rescaled profiles), CMB map filtering schemes, and noise levels.
AI.result: Void x CMB lensing signal is less sensitive to mock catalog choice than galaxy and void statistics. Highest S/N is achieved for 2D voids with rescaled profiles. Forecast: S/N ~13σ (2D) / 8σ (3D) with Planck, increasing to 22σ/13σ for SO and 31σ/18σ for CMB-S4-like surveys.
AI.conclusion: Void x CMB lensing is robust to mock construction choices, reducing risk of systematic tensions. Roman combined with next-generation LSS and CMB surveys opens a path toward the first direct cosmological constraints from Void x CMB lensing, though the cosmological dependence of the signal remains to be quantified.

title: Predicting intermediate-mass black hole formation in star clusters with machine learning
summary: Whether intermediate-mass black holes reside in nearby star clusters has remained contested for decades. We address this question by training neural network and random forest regressors on synthetic catalogs generated with the {\sc Rapster} cluster evolution code, mapping observable cluster properties such as total mass and half-mass radius onto the mass of the heaviest black hole built up through repeated mergers. Applying these models to nearby globular and nuclear star clusters, we forecast the intermediate-mass black hole population that each system may host. Globular clusters are unlikely to contain black holes more massive than $\sim 100\,M_\odot$, with an occupation fraction near 0.02, although they can produce remnants within the upper mass gap with masses approaching $100\,M_\odot$. Among nuclear star clusters, a handful of cases, including NGC 5102 and NGC 5206, yield predicted central black hole masses above $100\,M_\odot$, which we contrast with kinematically inferred estimates. Where the observationally claimed masses exceed our predictions, the implication is that the assembly history involved processes beyond hierarchical mergers, most plausibly accretion of gas and stars. Finally, we employ a normalizing flow to quantify, for individual globular clusters, the likelihood that their initial conditions were favorable to a collisional runaway during the first few million years after formation.

AI.tldr: The paper uses machine learning (neural networks and random forest regressors) trained on synthetic star cluster catalogs to predict the masses of black holes formed through repeated mergers in globular and nuclear star clusters. It finds globular clusters rarely host black holes >100 M☉ (occupation fraction ~0.02), while some nuclear star clusters may contain intermediate-mass black holes exceeding 100 M☉. Where observational claims exceed predictions, additional accretion processes beyond hierarchical mergers are implied.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing debate over whether intermediate-mass black holes reside in nearby star clusters by using machine learning models trained on simulated cluster evolution data to predict black hole masses.
AI.method: Neural network and random forest regressors were trained on synthetic catalogs from the Rapster cluster evolution code, mapping observable cluster properties (total mass, half-mass radius) to the mass of the heaviest black hole from repeated mergers. A normalizing flow was also used to assess the likelihood of collisional runaway in early cluster evolution.
AI.result: Globular clusters are unlikely to host black holes >100 M☉ (occupation fraction ~0.02) but can produce remnants in the upper mass gap near 100 M☉. Some nuclear star clusters (e.g., NGC 5102, NGC 5206) have predicted black hole masses >100 M☉. Discrepancies between predictions and kinematic estimates suggest additional accretion processes.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate-mass black holes in globular clusters are rare; where observational claims exceed model predictions, gas/stellar accretion beyond hierarchical mergers is likely required to explain the assembly history.

title: Primordial black holes in excursion set theory: Formation probabilities, mass functions, and window functions
summary: We study the mass function of primordial black holes (PBHs) within the excursion-set theory, in which the response of the stochastic density contrast to the variation of the coarse-graining scale is described by colored noises. For several window functions often used in the literature, we investigate how this choice affects the formation probability as well as the resultant mass function of PBHs. It is found that the low-mass tail of the mass function differs from the one predicted from Carr's formula. The difference comes from the prevalence of correlated noises, by which degeneracy of the formation probabilities ceases to exist. Nevertheless, Carr's formula still provides a practical estimation in the vicinity of the characteristic mass scale, as long as a smooth window function in Fourier space is used.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates PBH mass functions using excursion-set theory with colored noises, finding that the low-mass tail deviates from Carr's formula due to correlated noise effects, though Carr's formula remains practical near the characteristic mass scale when using smooth window functions in Fourier space.
AI.motivation: To understand how the choice of window functions and colored noises in excursion-set theory affects the formation probability and mass function of primordial black holes, particularly examining deviations from the widely used Carr's formula.
AI.method: Excursion-set theory framework with colored noises, analyzing the response of stochastic density contrast to coarse-graining scale variations using different window functions commonly employed in the literature.
AI.result: The low-mass tail of the PBH mass function differs from Carr's formula prediction due to correlated noises breaking the degeneracy of formation probabilities. However, Carr's formula still provides practical estimates near the characteristic mass scale when smooth Fourier-space window functions are used.
AI.conclusion: Carr's formula is not universally valid across all mass scales; the choice of window function and noise correlations significantly impacts PBH mass function predictions, especially at low masses.

title: Advancing the detection of low surface brightness galaxies. I. ATTILA: multi-tAsking deTecTIon tool for Lsb gAlaxies
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to A&A Comments are welcome The ATTILA code will be publicly available once the paper has been accepted
summary: Context. Ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) lie at the extreme end of the size-luminosity distribution of low surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies. Their detection and characterization require deep imaging and reliable source detection techniques that can handle low signal-to-noise ratios and severe source blending. Aims. We aim at improving the detection and characterization of the LSB galaxies and UDG candidates in different environments. To this end, we have developed a new automated detection Python-based tool, named ATTILA. Methods. We use deep g- and r-band imaging from the VST Early-type GAlaxy Survey (VEGAS), covering the central region of Hydra I and three new additional fields. Sources are identified combining tiling processing, source detection, and iterative deblending. The structural parameters are derived through surface brightness profile analysis and Sérsic modelling. Cluster membership is determined using the early-type galaxies colour-magnitude relation. Results. We identify 24 new UDGs, doubling the known population in the Hydra-I cluster to 48, consistent with expectations from halo mass scaling relations, and 92 additional LSB galaxies. In real data, ATTILA recovers more than 80% of previously known LSB galaxies and significantly improves the automated detection rate relative to standard methods. Conclusions. By improving the recovery of faint and diffuse sources while mitigating blending and contamination effects, ATTILA enables a more complete census of the LSB galaxy population, including UDGs.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ATTILA, a new Python-based automated tool for detecting and characterizing low surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies and ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) using deep VST VEGAS imaging. Applied to the Hydra I cluster, it identifies 24 new UDGs (doubling the known population to 48) and 92 additional LSB galaxies, achieving >80% recovery of known LSBs and improving automated detection over standard methods.
AI.motivation: Ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) represent an extreme population of low surface-brightness galaxies that are difficult to detect and characterize due to low signal-to-noise ratios and source blending. Improved detection techniques are needed to obtain a more complete census of LSB galaxies across different environments.
AI.method: A new automated Python tool (ATTILA) was developed, combining tiling processing, source detection, and iterative deblending on deep g- and r-band VST VEGAS imaging of Hydra I (central region + three new fields). Structural parameters were derived via surface brightness profile analysis and Sérsic modelling, and cluster membership was determined using the early-type galaxy colour-magnitude relation.
AI.result: 24 new UDGs were discovered, doubling the known Hydra I UDG population to 48 (consistent with halo mass scaling relations). Additionally, 92 LSB galaxies were identified. ATTILA recovered >80% of previously known LSB galaxies in real data and significantly outperformed standard automated detection methods.
AI.conclusion: ATTILA improves the recovery of faint, diffuse sources while mitigating blending and contamination, enabling a more complete census of the LSB and UDG population.

title: JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES) Data Release 5: stellar population catalogue for galaxies in GOODS-N and GOODS-S
summary: We present the galaxy stellar population catalogue from the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES) Data Release 5 (DR5), providing homogeneous Bayesian inference of physical galaxy properties in GOODS-N and GOODS-S. Using deep JWST/NIRCam and MIRI imaging combined with ancillary multi-wavelength data, we model the spectral energy distributions of ~500,000 sources with the Prospector framework. Our modelling incorporates flexible non-parametric star-formation histories (SFHs), nebular emission, dust attenuation, metallicities, and mid-infrared AGN and dust emission. We adopt an evolving star-forming main sequence (SFMS) prior for modelling the SFHs, which provides a physically-motivated long-term shape of SFHs while retaining non-parametric flexibility. The prior links stellar mass growth and SFR through the observed redshift-dependent SFMS, shaping the global behaviour of the inferred SFHs but allowing substantial deviations and scatters wherever supported by the data. We derive posterior distributions for stellar masses, SFRs, SFHs, dust attenuation, metallicities, and AGN contributions. The depth and wavelength coverage of JADES enable robust stellar mass measurements down to low-mass limits, as well as improved constraints on recent star-formation activity for ~350,000 galaxies at z = 1 - 9. The adoption of a physically motivated prior mitigates unphysical solutions and reduces degeneracies between redshift, age, dust, and metallicity, particularly for faint sources. We validate the catalogue through consistency checks and comparison to spectroscopic redshifts where available. The resulting value-added catalogue provides a uniform set of stellar population parameters suitable for statistical studies of galaxy growth, quenching, and the build-up of stellar mass across cosmic time. The full catalogue and posterior summaries are publicly released as part of JADES DR5.

AI.tldr: The JADES DR5 galaxy stellar population catalogue provides Bayesian inference of physical properties for ~500,000 sources in GOODS-N and GOODS-S using JWST/NIRCam+MIRI imaging and the Prospector framework. It employs an evolving star-forming main sequence prior for non-parametric SFHs, deriving stellar masses, SFRs, SFHs, dust attenuation, metallicities, and AGN contributions for galaxies at z=1-9. The catalogue is validated and publicly released.
AI.motivation: To provide a homogeneous, physically-robust, and publicly available stellar population catalogue from JWST deep extragalactic survey data, enabling statistical studies of galaxy growth, quenching, and stellar mass assembly across cosmic time.
AI.method: Spectral energy distribution modelling of ~500,000 sources using the Prospector framework with flexible non-parametric SFHs, nebular emission, dust attenuation, metallicities, and mid-infrared AGN/dust emission. An evolving star-forming main sequence (SFMS) prior links stellar mass growth and SFR via the observed redshift-dependent SFMS, shaping the global SFH behaviour while allowing data-driven deviations.
AI.result: Posterior distributions for stellar masses, SFRs, SFHs, dust attenuation, metallicities, and AGN contributions for ~350,000 galaxies at z=1-9, with robust stellar mass measurements down to low-mass limits and improved constraints on recent star-formation activity.
AI.conclusion: The physically motivated SFMS prior mitigates unphysical solutions and reduces degeneracies (redshift, age, dust, metallicity), particularly for faint sources. The resulting value-added catalogue provides a uniform dataset for statistical galaxy evolution studies and is publicly released as part of JADES DR5.

title: Milky Way Mapper decoded abundances -- II: From patterns to paths
summary: The element abundances of Milky Way disc stars encode entangled imprints of multiple enrichment processes, making it difficult to uncover the underlying chemical evolution. Here we re-project 16 stellar abundances for 199,290 red giant stars ([Fe/H]$ > -1$) into a set of (4) shared enrichment patterns, providing a generative framework for learning the organising structure of the Milky Way disc. The relative contributions of these patterns vary systematically across the disc, revealing a low-dimensional enrichment basis that responds coherently to global drivers of disc evolution. By grouping stars according to their pattern contributions, we identify coherent enrichment pathways that exhibit strong chemo-spatial correlations and are stratified in both age and height above the plane, linking radial growth to vertical disc structure. Stars occupying similar positions along these enrichment pathways also show coherent vertical deviations across radius, indicating that the low-dimensional chemical structure captures the disc's response to dynamical perturbations. We identify a transition in enrichment behaviour at approximately 6 Gyr, marking the onset of a more chemically mixed regime with increasing contributions from delayed sources. Within this connected system, the observed $α$-bimodality arises within a shared, low-dimensional abundance structure, with stars populating continuous sequences of changing enrichment fractions that are tightly coupled to spatial, temporal, and orbital coordinates across the Milky Way disc.

AI.tldr: The authors decompose 16 stellar abundances from 199,290 red giant stars into 4 shared enrichment patterns, revealing a low-dimensional chemical structure that systematically varies across the Milky Way disc and correlates with age, height, and dynamical perturbations.
AI.motivation: Element abundances of Milky Way disc stars contain entangled enrichment processes that obscure the underlying chemical evolution; the authors aim to uncover the organizing structure by reducing high-dimensional abundance data into interpretable, low-dimensional enrichment patterns.
AI.method: They re-project 16 stellar abundances from 199,290 red giant stars ([Fe/H] > -1) into a set of 4 shared enrichment patterns using a generative framework, then group stars by pattern contributions to identify enrichment pathways and analyze chemo-spatial correlations.
AI.result: The 4 enrichment patterns vary systematically across the disc; stars grouped by these patterns exhibit strong chemo-spatial correlations stratified in age and height; a transition at ~6 Gyr marks onset of chemically mixed regime; the α-bimodality arises within this low-dimensional structure.
AI.conclusion: The Milky Way disc's chemical evolution is governed by a low-dimensional enrichment basis that responds coherently to global drivers, linking radial growth, vertical structure, and dynamical perturbations within a unified framework.

title: Dwarf Galaxy Constraints on Interacting Fermionic Dark Matter
summary: Dwarf galaxies in the Local Group offer a way to test dark matter (DM) models against stellar kinematic data. In this work, we study degenerate fermionic DM in two cases: the standard non-interacting Fermi gas, and an interacting degenerate DM fluid described by a phenomenological equation of state motivated by interacting Fermi systems. These interactions modify the compressibility of the DM fluid and, in some regions of parameter space, lead to mechanically unstable branches that must be treated through a Maxwell construction. We solve the corresponding non-relativistic hydrostatic equations consistently and compute the line-of-sight velocity-dispersion profiles using the spherical Jeans equation. We then perform MCMC fits to eight classical Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies. The data favor DM fermion masses in the range $100$--$300\,{\rm eV}$. We find that the interacting and non-interacting equations of state give broadly similar posterior distributions for the fermion mass, central density, and stellar anisotropy. Current data therefore do not strongly prefer an interacting equation of state over the free degenerate Fermi-gas, thereby excluding large deviations from the non-interacting limit.

AI.tldr: This paper tests degenerate fermionic dark matter models (both non-interacting and interacting) against stellar kinematic data from eight Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies, finding fermion masses in the 100–300 eV range and no strong preference for interacting over non-interacting equations of state.
AI.motivation: To test dark matter models using stellar kinematic data from Local Group dwarf galaxies, specifically comparing non-interacting and interacting degenerate fermionic DM scenarios.
AI.method: The authors solved non-relativistic hydrostatic equations with two equations of state (non-interacting Fermi gas and interacting Fermi fluid with phenomenological EoS), applied Maxwell construction for mechanically unstable branches, computed line-of-sight velocity-dispersion profiles via spherical Jeans equation, and performed MCMC fits to eight classical Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies.
AI.result: Data favor DM fermion masses in 100–300 eV range. Interacting and non-interacting equations of state yield broadly similar posterior distributions for fermion mass, central density, and stellar anisotropy. Current data do not strongly prefer an interacting EoS over the free degenerate Fermi gas.
AI.conclusion: Large deviations from the non-interacting degenerate Fermi gas limit are excluded by current stellar kinematic data from dwarf spheroidal galaxies.

title: Powerful Radio Sources in the Southern Sky. IV. Observations of the G4Jy-3CRE Catalog with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder
summary: A recent 2023 paper by Massaro et al. introduced the G4Jy-3CRE, a new catalog of the brightest radio sources in the southern hemisphere that serve as a southern equivalent to the Third Cambridge Catalog Revised (3CR). The G4Jy-3CRE catalog selected 264 sources from the GLEAM-4Jy survey based on the same criteria used to select the sources in the 3CR. In this paper, we present new Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) continuuum imaging of the G4Jy-3CRE catalog. We use the three most recent data releases from the Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey (RACS), covering the sky south of +30°decl.: RACS-low1, RACS-mid, and RACS-high. Together, these data releases cover a range of frequencies from 600 to 1800 MHz. The RACS surveys have improved spatial resolution and sensitivity over archival surveys at the same frequency, enabling us to classify 173 sources (66% of the sample) with morphologies indicative of the presence of jets, 37 of which did not show jet activity on archival radio maps. We were able to effectively classify FRI/FRII galaxies up to a redshift of z = 1.35. Moreover, we identified six optical counterparts for sources that were either previously unidentified or ambiguous.

AI.tldr: This paper presents new ASKAP continuum imaging of the G4Jy-3CRE catalog (264 southern radio sources), using RACS survey data (600-1800 MHz). The improved resolution/sensitivity allowed classification of 173 sources (66%) as jet-related morphologies (37 newly identified), FRI/FRII classification up to z=1.35, and optical identification of six previously unidentified sources.
AI.motivation: To provide a southern hemisphere equivalent to the 3CR catalog and characterize the G4Jy-3CRE sources with higher-resolution, multi-frequency ASKAP observations to reveal jet morphologies and identify optical counterparts previously unresolved or undetected.
AI.method: Used three RACS data releases (RACS-low1, RACS-mid, RACS-high) covering 600-1800 MHz for ASKAP continuum imaging of 264 G4Jy-3CRE sources; classified morphologies via visual inspection for jet signatures and FRI/FRII classification; identified optical counterparts through cross-matching.
AI.result: 173 sources (66%) showed jet-related morphologies (37 new detections of jet activity); FRI/FRII classification achieved up to z=1.35; six new optical counterparts identified for previously unidentified/ambiguous sources.
AI.conclusion: ASKAP/RACS surveys significantly improve the morphological classification and optical identification of southern radio sources, demonstrating the value of high-resolution, multi-frequency continuum imaging for studying radio-loud AGN populations.

title: From protogalaxy through thick and thin: Why did the Milky Way evolve in three kinematic phases?
summary: APOGEE and Gaia data have revealed that the Milky Way's structure appears to have evolved through three distinct kinematic phases. First, at early cosmic times, the Milky Way was a disordered protogalaxy, which subsequently "spun up" to a second kinematic phase marked by star formation occurring in a rotating, thick stellar disk. The thick disk phase later transitioned to a third (and final) phase with star formation occurring in a cold, thin stellar disk. In this paper, we use a suite of FIRE-2 simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies to demonstrate that the same three phases arise in our cosmological zoom-in simulations, and study their physical origin. In all of our galaxies, the early disordered phase occurs when the rate of cool gas ($T \leq 10^4$ K) converting into stars is low, the star formation rate is bursty, and the baryonic mass "sloshes" within the host potential with respect to the center of mass motion. The gas in the galaxy begins to spin coherently after the sloshing phase ends, followed by the spin-up of young stars. The central potential of the galaxy is least concentrated just prior to gas spin-up. This second, thick disk phase coincides with a period when the rate of cool gas converting into stars is highest, even though the star formation rate remains bursty in this phase. The final transition to the thin disk phase occurs when the inner circumgalactic medium virializes. The thin disk phase is associated with a time of steady star formation and intermediate rates of cool gas converting into stars. Mergers do not appear to play a defining role in driving transitions between the three phases. The condition for the formation of a thick disk appears to be fairly minimal: a stable center of mass motion. The formation of a thin disk requires more: gas must accrete slowly enough for its angular momentum to mix and become coherent prior to joining the galaxy.

AI.tldr: Using FIRE-2 simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies, the authors confirm that the Milky Way's structural evolution progresses through three kinematic phases: a disordered protogalaxy, a rotating thick disk, and a cold thin disk, driven by gas accretion dynamics and center-of-mass stability rather than mergers.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origin of the three distinct kinematic phases (disordered protogalaxy → thick disk → thin disk) observed in the Milky Way from APOGEE and Gaia data, using cosmological zoom-in simulations to identify driving mechanisms.
AI.method: Analyzed a suite of FIRE-2 cosmological zoom-in simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies, tracking kinematic phases, star formation burstiness, gas cooling rates, center-of-mass motion sloshing, circumgalactic medium virialization, and accretion dynamics across cosmic time.
AI.result: All simulated galaxies exhibit the same three phases. The disordered phase coincides with bursty star formation and baryonic sloshing. The thick disk forms after sloshing ends, with high cool-gas-to-star conversion rates despite bursty SF. The thin disk emerges when the inner CGM virializes, enabling steady SF and coherent angular momentum mixing. Mergers are not the primary drivers of phase transitions.
AI.conclusion: The thick disk requires only stable center-of-mass motion; the thin disk additionally requires slow gas accretion that allows angular momentum to mix and become coherent before joining the galaxy. Mergers do not define the transitions.

title: An AGN in the Antennae galaxies ?
summary: Time variability is a strong probe of energetic phenomena which occur at small spatial scales, like Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN). We use ALMA observations at 100 GHz executed over a period of 2.5 months to look for time variability in the Antennae galaxies, a prototypical early stage merger galaxy pair, for which there are no previous signatures of an AGN in the optical, infrared or X-ray. Most 100 GHz detections in the Antennae are spatially extended and associated with star forming regions, but two sources in the southern galaxy NGC 4039 are compact. One of these compact sources, S3, is offset by 1 arcsecond in the northeast direction from the stellar peak of NGC 4039, and marginally resolved at 10 parsec resolution. The other source, S4, is co-spatial with the stellar peak of NGC 4039 and unresolved even at a resolution of 4 parsec. We examine the time variability of these two sources using their power spectrum. We find that S4 varies with a characteristic timescale of 13+/-3 days, indicating that the phenomena responsible for the 100 GHz emission is smaller than 0.01 parsecs. By comparing the observed flux of the two sources with various candidate origins, we show that while S3 can be explained either by a young massive stellar cluster or an AGN, S4 is likely to be an AGN that is possibly Compton-thick.

AI.tldr: Using ALMA 100 GHz observations over 2.5 months, the authors detect two compact sources (S3 and S4) in the Antennae galaxies merger. S4 shows 13-day variability, is unresolved at 4 pc, and is likely a Compton-thick AGN, while S3 could be either a young stellar cluster or an AGN.
AI.motivation: Time variability is a powerful probe of small-scale energetic phenomena like AGNs. The Antennae galaxies—a prototypical early-stage merger—had no prior AGN signatures in optical, IR, or X-ray bands, making high-frequency radio variability a novel way to search for hidden AGN activity.
AI.method: ALMA 100 GHz observations over 2.5 months; power spectrum analysis to assess variability timescales; comparison of observed fluxes with candidate origins (young stellar clusters vs. AGN).
AI.result: Two compact sources identified: S3 (marginally resolved at 10 pc, offset from stellar peak) and S4 (unresolved at 4 pc, co-spatial with stellar peak). S4 varies with a characteristic timescale of 13±3 days, implying emission region <0.01 pc. S3 shows no strong variability.
AI.conclusion: S4 is likely a Compton-thick AGN; S3 may be either a young massive stellar cluster or an AGN. The discovery demonstrates that mm-wave variability can reveal hidden AGNs in mergers where other wavelengths show no signatures.

title: Silicate cosmic dust grain collisions in the interstellar medium: A molecular dynamics study
comment: To be submitted to A&A, comments welcome
summary: (abridged) We aim to predict the most important parameters for grain-grain collision outcomes for models of interstellar grain population evolution on astrophysical scales: the threshold velocity above which colliding grains shatter, the threshold for vaporization, and resulting distributions of grain sizes. We use molecular dynamics simulations which evolve the dynamics of each atom in a dust grain to explore the outcomes of collisions between silicate grains of radii $a \in [5,50]~Å$ at velocities $0.1-20$ km/s. We run simulations of grains with two materials: amorphous SiO$_2$ and an amorphous silicate of composition suggested by Draine \& Hensley (2021). With these simulations, we quantify the collision velocity dependence of shattered and vaporized mass fractions, and the resulting size distributions of shattering products. We find grain shattering thresholds are $\sim$6 km/s for both amorphous SiO$_2$ and astrodust material, which is a factor of $\sim$2 higher than the canonical value for silicates of 2.7 km/s from Jones et al. (1996). This discrepancy is mostly alleviated by correcting an error in the expression for these velocity thresholds derived in Tielens et al. (1994). We find that the size distributions of shattered products are generally not consistent with the power law distributions predicted by this previous model. We also find that their expression fails to predict the fraction of shattered or vaporized material observed in our numerical simulations. The model of Hirashita \& Kobayashi (2013) for the same quantities similarly fails to match the simulations. We provide updated shattering velocity thresholds for standard candidate grain materials to the astrophysics community. Broadly, our updated threshold velocities that astrophysical dust grains may be more robust to shattering in the interstellar medium than previously assumed.

AI.tldr: Molecular dynamics simulations of silicate grain collisions (5-50 Å radii, 0.1-20 km/s) show shattering thresholds ~6 km/s—~2× higher than canonical 2.7 km/s—due to an error in Tielens et al. (1994). Shattered size distributions deviate from power-law predictions, and existing models (Jones et al., Hirashita & Kobayashi) fail to match simulated mass fractions. Updated thresholds suggest interstellar grains are more robust to shattering than previously assumed.
AI.motivation: To accurately predict key parameters (shattering/vaporization thresholds and size distributions) for grain-grain collisions in models of interstellar grain population evolution on astrophysical scales, as prior theoretical thresholds may be erroneous.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics simulations tracking individual atom dynamics in collisions of amorphous SiO₂ and Draine & Hensley (2021) astrodust silicate grains (radii 5–50 Å) across velocities 0.1–20 km/s, quantifying shattered/vaporized mass fractions and product size distributions.
AI.result: Shattering thresholds ~6 km/s for both materials, ~2× higher than Jones et al. (1996) canonical value of 2.7 km/s, primarily due to an error in Tielens et al. (1994) velocity threshold expression. Size distributions of shattered products are inconsistent with power-law predictions from previous models; neither Jones et al. nor Hirashita & Kobayashi (2013) models correctly predict shattered/vaporized fractions.
AI.conclusion: Updated shattering velocity thresholds are provided; interstellar dust grains appear more robust to shattering than previously thought, necessitating revisions to dust evolution models.

title: MICONIC: The multiphase circumnuclear region of Centaurus A as seen with JWST/MIRI MRS observations. I. Spectral inventory and properties of the warm molecular disk
summary: Supermassive black holes power Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), injecting energy that regulates accretion and shapes host galaxies. We investigate the morphology, excitation, and kinematics of molecular hydrogen (H2) in the inner circumnuclear disk of Centaurus A, the nearest radio galaxy. We present JWST/MIRI MRS integral-field spectroscopy of the central 170x100 pc2 at 0.3"-0.7" (5-12 pc) resolution, focusing on pure rotational H2 lines. The spectra show strong nuclear continuum and bright H2 emission from S(1) to S(8), including the first S(8) detection in Centaurus A. Optically thin nuclear lines enable maps of temperature, column density, and ortho-to-para ratio from spaxel-level excitation-diagram fitting. Warm H2 shows a complex morphology, dominating the central region where CO emission is weak or undetected. Low-excitation H2 lines trace an inhomogeneous ring with a 20-pc-radius cavity aligned with the jet's near side, suggesting that the jet affects the morphology of the molecular disk. Higher-excitation lines form filamentary structures around the AGN. Kinematics are rotational with an S-shaped distortion, indicating non-circular motions or a warped disk. A coherent, low-dispersion (70 km/s) streamer spirals inward. A power-law temperature distribution yields a warm (100-2000 K) H2 mass of (5.6+/-1.4)e5 Msun and a dynamical mass of 5e8 Msun within 100 pc. Shock excitation is supported by enhanced H2/continuum and H2/PAH ratios, elevated [Ne III]/[Ne II], and sub-equilibrium ortho-to-para ratios (1.6-2.4). Turbulent dissipation can balance H2 cooling and likely dominates heating beyond 30 pc. In the inner 100 pc of Centaurus A, AGN feeding and feedback are linked: shocks excite H2, regulate the gas temperature, and prevent cooling below 100 K, explaining the weak CO emission and lack of a massive outflow. These shocks may drive angular momentum loss and help fuel the nucleus.

AI.tldr: JWST/MIRI MRS observations of Centaurus A's inner 170×100 pc reveal warm H₂ emission with complex morphology, rotational kinematics with S-shaped distortion, and an inward-spiraling streamer. Shock excitation dominates, regulating gas temperature above 100 K and suppressing CO emission, linking AGN feeding and feedback through shock-driven angular momentum loss.
AI.motivation: To understand how supermassive black holes power AGN and regulate accretion and host galaxy evolution, by studying the morphology, excitation, and kinematics of warm molecular hydrogen in the innermost circumnuclear disk of the nearest radio galaxy, Centaurus A.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI MRS integral-field spectroscopy at 0.3"-0.7" (5-12 pc) resolution covering 170×100 pc², focusing on pure rotational H₂ lines S(1)–S(8). Spaxel-level excitation-diagram fitting to derive temperature, column density, and ortho-to-para ratio maps. Kinematic and morphological analysis of H₂ line emission.
AI.result: First S(8) detection in Centaurus A. Warm H₂ dominates where CO is weak/absent. Low-excitation lines trace an inhomogeneous ring with a 20-pc cavity aligned with the jet's near side; higher-excitation lines form filaments around the AGN. Rotational kinematics show S-shaped distortion and a low-dispersion (70 km/s) inward-spiraling streamer. Warm (100–2000 K) H₂ mass of (5.6±1.4)×10⁵ M☉, dynamical mass of 5×10⁸ M☉ within 100 pc. Enhanced H₂/continuum, H₂/PAH, elevated [Ne III]/[Ne II], and sub-equilibrium ortho-to-para ratios (1.6–2.4) indicate shock excitation. Turbulent dissipation likely dominates heating beyond 30 pc.
AI.conclusion: Shocks from AGN feedback excite H₂, regulate gas temperature, and prevent cooling below 100 K, explaining the weak CO emission and lack of massive outflow. Shocks may drive angular momentum loss to fuel the nucleus, linking AGN feeding and feedback in the inner 100 pc of Centaurus A.

title: The habitability trade-off: Chemical decoupling and quenching in massive galaxies
comment: accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Massive galaxies experience complex evolutionary processes, including mergers and gas accretion, which can disrupt the chemical equilibrium between their stellar and gaseous components. Using the IllustrisTNG (TNG100) simulation at $z=0$, we investigated the prevalence and physical properties of such chemically decoupled systems within the massive star-forming galaxy population.
