We identify a substantial subpopulation ($\sim 31.5\%$ of the sample) that exhibits systematic stellar-gas decoupling, characterised by a metal-rich stellar component coexisting with a diluted gas reservoir. These non-equilibrium galaxies are closely linked to recent merger activity and partial quenching, and display systematically suppressed star-formation rates and reduced gas fractions, consistent with a transitional evolutionary phase. We then examined the implications of this phase for galaxy-scale habitability prescriptions by applying a terrestrial planet abundance proxy that combines stellar mass, gas-phase metallicity, and the rate of sterilising events. Despite their diluted gas reservoirs, non-equilibrium galaxies dominate the high end of the inferred present-day habitability proxy distribution, exceeding equilibrium systems by more than an order of magnitude. We interpret this as a habitability trade-off: the same gas dilution and quenching processes that reduce the efficiency of future terrestrial planet formation simultaneously create a transient phase of suppressed radiation hazards for existing planets. The Andromeda galaxy (M31) shows qualitative similarities to this chemically decoupled population, suggesting that galaxies exiting their peak star-forming phase represent a distinct and highly relevant demographic for galaxy-scale habitability. Galactic habitability is therefore intrinsically time-dependent.

AI.tldr: Using TNG100 simulations, ~31.5% of massive star-forming galaxies at z=0 show chemical decoupling (metal-rich stars, diluted gas), linked to mergers/partial quenching. Despite suppressed star formation, these non-equilibrium galaxies dominate the high end of present-day habitability proxy distributions due to reduced radiation hazards, highlighting the time-dependent nature of galactic habitability.
AI.motivation: To investigate the prevalence and physical properties of chemically decoupled systems (where stellar and gaseous components are out of equilibrium) in massive star-forming galaxies, and to understand their implications for galaxy-scale habitability.
AI.method: Analyzed the IllustrisTNG (TNG100) simulation at z=0, identified non-equilibrium galaxies via stellar-gas decoupling (metal-rich stars + diluted gas), examined their link to merger activity and partial quenching, and applied a terrestrial planet abundance proxy combining stellar mass, gas-phase metallicity, and sterilizing event rate.
AI.result: ~31.5% of the sample exhibits systematic stellar-gas decoupling; these galaxies show suppressed SFRs and reduced gas fractions, linked to recent mergers and partial quenching. Despite diluted gas reservoirs, they dominate the high end of the habitability proxy distribution, exceeding equilibrium systems by >1 order of magnitude. M31 shows qualitative similarities.
AI.conclusion: Galactic habitability is intrinsically time-dependent. A transient phase of suppressed radiation hazards for existing planets arises from the same gas dilution and quenching processes that reduce future terrestrial planet formation efficiency. Galaxies exiting their peak star-forming phase represent a distinct and relevant demographic for habitability studies.

title: Probing the ion-neutral drift velocity towards the L1544 prestellar core: Detection of ambipolar diffusion using N$_2$D$^+$ and para-NH$_2$D
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The dynamical role of the magnetic field in the star formation process is tightly linked to the coupling between matter and the field. This coupling is due to the interaction between ions and neutrals in the partially ionized interstellar medium. When the ionization degree drops in the dense environment of prestellar cores, the magnetic field and the matter may decouple, leading to differences in the infalling velocities of ions and neutrals known as ambipolar diffusion. The onset of gravitational collapse resulting from ion-neutral decoupling has never been observed. The aim of this work is to search for signatures of ambipolar diffusion within a prestellar core. We observed the deuterated N$_2$D$^+$ ion and the neutral para-NH$_2$D species towards the prototypical prestellar core L1544. These two species are ideal tracers of prestellar cores sampling the same high densities in the core interior. We compared the velocity centroid and linewidth maps of the ion-neutral pair. We find a mean ion-neutral velocity difference of $\sim$0.05 km/s towards the core. By comparing with predictions from self-consistent calculations of the ambipolar resistivity including dust grain growth, we interpret the observed ion-neutral velocity difference in L1544 as a signature of ambipolar diffusion. We do not detect a significant ion-neutral linewidth difference that may be attributed to the subsonic infall motions of the gas in L1544 and geometrical effects in the presence of inclination. These results emphasize the role of dust grain growth at the prestellar core stage in setting the ambipolar resistivity and regulating the dynamical evolution of dense cores towards their collapse into protostars. We propose that measurements of ion-neutral drift velocities provide new constraints on the total magnetic field strength and the dust size distribution within prestellar cores.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first observational detection of ambipolar diffusion (ion-neutral velocity drift) in the prestellar core L1544, using N₂D⁺ and para-NH₂D as tracer species, finding a mean velocity difference of ~0.05 km/s consistent with theoretical models including dust grain growth.
AI.motivation: The onset of gravitational collapse resulting from ion-neutral decoupling (ambipolar diffusion) has never been observed; the work aims to search for signatures of ambipolar diffusion within a prestellar core.
AI.method: Observations of deuterated N₂D⁺ (ion) and neutral para-NH₂D species towards the prototypical prestellar core L1544, comparing velocity centroid and linewidth maps of this ion-neutral pair.
AI.result: Mean ion-neutral velocity difference of ~0.05 km/s detected; no significant ion-neutral linewidth difference attributable to subsonic infall motions and geometrical effects with inclination.
AI.conclusion: The observed velocity difference is interpreted as a signature of ambipolar diffusion, emphasizing the role of dust grain growth in setting ambipolar resistivity and regulating dynamical evolution; measurements of ion-neutral drift velocities provide new constraints on magnetic field strength and dust size distribution in prestellar cores.

title: Mass Segregation in the CMZoom Survey
summary: We employ a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) approach to characterize the spatial distribution and mass segregation of compact millimeter continuum sources within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way. We use a modified form of the complete version of the 1.3 mm dust continuum catalog from the CMZoom survey, which identifies 685 compact sources with typical effective radii of $\sim0.1$ pc. For 22 of 35 CMZ clouds, we calculate the thermal and turbulent Jeans lengths and masses, and determine that compact source separations, as well as compact source masses, are more consistent with thermal fragmentation at $\sim0.1$ pc size scales. We construct the mass segregation ratios for compact sources in 17 CMZ clouds and determine that 5 of the analyzed clouds display some form of mass segregation ($Λ_{MSR} > 1.5$), while the remaining clouds show either inverse mass segregation ($Λ_{MSR} < 0.75$), or no evidence of true mass segregation ($0.75 < Λ_{MSR} < 1.5$). Finally, we find that although some actively star-forming clouds do exhibit mass segregation, other similarly active clouds do not, indicating an unclear correlation with evolutionary stage for star forming clouds in the CMZ, given the current available data.

AI.tldr: Using an MST approach on 685 compact mm sources from CMZoom, the authors find that source separations and masses in CMZ clouds are consistent with thermal fragmentation at ~0.1 pc scales. Mass segregation analysis shows only 5 of 17 clouds exhibit segregation (Λ_MSR > 1.5), with no clear correlation to evolutionary stage.
AI.motivation: To characterize the spatial distribution and mass segregation of compact millimeter continuum sources within the CMZ, and to understand the fragmentation physics (thermal vs. turbulent) governing star formation in this extreme environment.
AI.method: MST approach applied to a modified CMZoom 1.3 mm dust continuum catalog (685 compact sources). Calculated thermal/turbulent Jeans lengths and masses for 22 clouds, and mass segregation ratios (Λ_MSR) for 17 clouds.
AI.result: Compact source separations and masses are more consistent with thermal fragmentation at ~0.1 pc. Only 5 out of 17 clouds show mass segregation (Λ_MSR > 1.5); others show inverse or no segregation. Correlation with evolutionary stage is unclear.
AI.conclusion: Thermal fragmentation dominates at ~0.1 pc scales in the CMZ. Mass segregation is not universal among CMZ clouds and does not clearly correlate with star formation activity or evolutionary stage given current data.
